newsitem.title: USA: W.House to reject key element of tobacco deal - Post.
newsitem.headline: W.House to reject key element of tobacco deal - Post.

text.p: The White House will reject a key element of the proposed $368 billion tobacco settlement because it would impose new restrictions on federal authority to regulate nicotine in cigarettes, the Washington Post reported Wednesday.

The newspaper quoted senior officials as saying the Clinton administration had decided to reject part of the deal after concluding that it surrendered too much of the Food and Drug Administration's ability to control the addictiveness of cigarettes.
Such limits would roll back the administration's campaign to assert jurisdiction over tobacco, the officials said.

Aides to President Clinton planned to rewrite the proposal themselves and said the president was willing to walk away from the settlement proposal entirely if he cannot amend it to his satisfaction, the newspaper said.
"After taking a serious look at it, (the proposals) are unacceptable," one administration told the paper. "The way it's written, it actually slides back on what we've already won."

Under the agreement reached last month between the industry and 40 states suing it, tobacco companies would pay out $368 billion over 25 years. Some of that money would fund public health anti-smoking initiatives.

During months of tough negotiations, the tobacco companies insisted that the FDA meet certain standards before being allowed to reduce nicotine in cigarettes, including complying with a requirement that it prove such a move would not create a black market in stronger cigarettes.
Tobacco companies executives last week met with White House advisers and were not enthusiastic about reopening negotiations on the settlement, but they also did not rule out further concessions.

The Post quoted Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore, who led the negotiations with the tobacco companies, as saying that too much tinkering with the deal "runs a great chance of running the industry off."
Officials said that they believe it is now up to them to craft legislation to send Congress, rather than sending the attorneys general and tobacco executives back to the bargaining table.

A team of prominent public health experts and anti-smoking activists led by former U.S. Surgeon General C. Everett Koop and former Food and Drug Administration chief David Kessler will deliver a report critical of the agreement to a White House task force Wednesday.

The Koop-Kessler criticisms are likely to carry weight in the White House, which is conducting a 30-day review of the proposed settlement, and in Congress, which would have to approve legislation to enact a deal.
